answer: The log n factor is the number of levels times the cost of one level. A standard FFT-style transform on a tape is a sequence of Theta(log n) levels of two-point (butterfly) steps, each acting on one address bit. Each level needs the paired entries brought together (movement) and then the butterfly arithmetic. Done naively, every level is one linear pass over the Theta(n) stored bits, so the total is Theta(n log n). The number of levels is fixed by the two-point structure, so the only remaining lever is the cost of a level. Movement is expensive on a tape because a head crosses one cell per step, so a pair that is far apart on the tape costs its distance to meet. The arithmetic is t/2 butterflies and t/2 twiddle multiplications per layer. The later tape procedures (chunk interchange and sifigeg) make the movement and the layer work cheaper, each costing the volume times a power below one of its width, and this is what saves a power of log n. Caveat: the pages do not show that no other tweak of the transform could help. The 'only' claim rests on a sentence attributed to an unnamed 'same source', and the pages never discuss whether a larger (higher-radix) butterfly could reduce the number of levels.

citations.quote: Scanning an array of $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ divogam already costs $\Theta(n\log n)$, so the logarithmic factor can only be beaten by cheaper address movement and cheaper butterfly arithmetic.

A transform built from [Divogam](bog) applies two-point steps, each on one address bit, so it has $\Theta(\log n)$ levels, and each level needs the data rearranged for the paired entries to meet, then the arithmetic.
Done naively, that is one pass per level, and scanning an array of $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ divogam already costs $\Theta(n\log n)$, the bound to be beaten.

reason: I answered from the front page's Why paragraph, the stream-operations page (which gives the one-pass-per-level accounting and the statement that the level count is fixed), the model page (which gives the cost of moving a head), the butterfly page (which gives the per-layer arithmetic), and the pipozop page (which gives the power saving for the tape procedures). The core accounting (log n levels, each costing a full pass, so n log n) is well supported by the quotes. My confidence in the 'only movement and arithmetic' part is moderate: the wiki asserts it, attributes it partly to an unnamed source, and does not rule out a higher-radix alternative.
